name: Shrug Whatever
description: A dismissive pair that combines a full shrug with a one-handed wave-off. Used to say 'I don't know and I don't care' or to deflect from a problem that isn't yours.
meaning: 🤷💁 stacks two palm-up gestures: the shrug that says nobody knows, followed by the hand-tip that says not my problem. Together they read as a refusal to engage—the first emoji admits the uncertainty, the second one brushes it away. It lands softer than either alone.
examples: asked my roommate if she knew where my keys were 🤷💁
so apparently there's a meeting tomorrow? 🤷💁 nobody told me about it
he said he wasn't coming but also didn't tell anyone else so 🤷💁
the project deadline got moved again 🤷💁 not like i had plans anyway
my mom keeps asking why i'm still single 🤷💁 idk either
seoDescription: What does 🤷💁 mean? It's a dismissive combo that says 'I don't know and I don't care'—used to deflect from problems that aren't yours.

longForm.overview:
🤷💁 is the combo for saying 'this is not my problem and also nobody knows what's happening.' The shrug raises both palms—a gesture that admits confusion or indifference. The hand-tip follows with one palm out, the gesture servers use to say 'can I help you with anything else?' but deployed here as a dismissal: not my department.

The pair works because it lets the sender acknowledge something without taking responsibility for it. A single 🤷 can read as apologetic; a single 💁 can read as offering help. Together they read as pure deflection. You see it when someone is commenting on a situation they're not part of, when a plan falls apart and nobody knows why, or when someone else's mistake becomes everyone's problem—except yours.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
🤷💁 shows up in group chats when the chaos is not your chaos. A friend cancels plans and nobody knows the reason—you send 🤷💁. A work project gets delayed because someone dropped the ball and nobody's saying who—you send 🤷💁. It pairs naturally with sentences that start with 'apparently,' 'supposedly,' or 'so I guess.' The combo reads as lighthearted; it is not angry, just completely unbothered.

It works best when you are reporting secondhand information or reacting to someone else's failure. Send it when you want to seem above the drama without actually leaving the conversation. It is the emoji equivalent of raising your hand and saying 'that's above my pay grade.'
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Skip 🤷💁 when the problem actually is your problem. If you forgot to do something, a 🤷💁 reads as flippant instead of apologetic. If someone is asking you for help and you send 🤷💁, they will read it as you refusing—which you are, but it lands harsher than you probably mean.

Avoid it in contexts where the receiver might think you are mocking them. A friend tells you they messed up and you reply 🤷💁, the combo reads as 'your mistake is not my concern' rather than 'I'm not judging you.' If the situation is serious, reach for a plain sentence or 💀 if you want to keep the deflection playful.
longForm.howToReply:
If you receive 🤷💁, you can mirror it back if you also don't know what's happening. If the sender is deflecting from something you actually need them to care about, a simple 'lol okay but seriously' or 'fair' acknowledges the joke and moves the conversation forward. The combo is usually not the end of a thought—it is a beat between confusion and moving on.

If someone sends 🤷💁 to you after you've asked them for help, they are telling you they cannot or will not help. Asking again rarely changes that. If you need their actual help, drop the playfulness and ask directly. If you just needed to vent, the combo is their way of saying they heard you and they're not taking it personally.

faqs.question: Is 🤷💁 rude or is it just joking around?
faqs.answer: It depends on context. Between friends it reads as lighthearted deflection. In a work channel or to someone who actually needs your help, it reads as a refusal. The tone lives in the sentence around it—'idk 🤷💁' to a friend is joking; 'idk 🤷💁' to a coworker asking for a deadline is dismissive.

faqs.question: What's the difference between 🤷💁 and just 🤷?
faqs.answer: A single 🤷 admits confusion or indifference. 🤷💁 adds a layer of deflection—it says not only do I not know, but also this is not my responsibility. The second emoji transforms the first from uncertainty into dismissal.

faqs.question: Can you use 🤷💁 in a work message?
faqs.answer: Carefully. It works in friendly team channels when you're commenting on someone else's chaos. Never send it to a manager or client. In a work setting it reads as you refusing accountability, which can land you in trouble if the reader thinks the problem should be yours.

faqs.question: What should I send instead if 🤷💁 seems too cold?
faqs.answer: If you want to deflect but sound warmer, try 🤷 alone or 💀 to show you think the situation is absurd. If you actually want to help, drop the emoji and just say so. If you genuinely don't know and don't care, 🤷💁 is doing exactly what you mean.

conversationExamples.message: the client asked for the redesign three weeks early and apparently it's happening 🤷💁 nobody asked me though
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is reporting a change that affects everyone but insisting it doesn't affect their workload. This reads as protective—they're saying 'I heard this is happening but I'm not committing to it.' A coworker might reply 'lol same energy' if they also heard about it secondhand, or 'okay but are you actually doing it' if they need confirmation.

conversationExamples.message: he said he was busy but didn't say with what so 🤷💁 his loss
conversationExamples.interpretation: A friend is reporting that someone flaked or was vague about their availability. The sender is unbothered and moving on. The appropriate response is to validate the 'his loss' energy by agreeing or suggesting something else to do instead.

conversationExamples.message: matched with him but his first message was 'hey' and nothing else so 🤷💁
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is dismissing someone's low-effort message. This reads as 'I'm not interested enough to carry this conversation.' If you're a friend, you can reply with 💀 or 'lmao the bar is in hell' to validate the dismissal. Do not try to convince them the person was worth responding to.

conversationExamples.message: apparently mom's side of the family is coming to thanksgiving but like nobody confirmed anything so 🤷💁
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is reporting family drama or vagueness without taking ownership of figuring it out. They're saying 'this is confusing and I'm not making phone calls about it.' A family member might reply 'yeah i heard something about that too' to commiserate, or you might ask a clarifying question only if you actually need to know.

conversationExamples.message: someone said they were starting a group chat for the trip but never actually sent the link so 🤷💁 guess we're winging it
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is commenting on a failure of coordination without taking blame for it. They're saying 'this is chaotic and I'm okay with that.' The appropriate response is to either laugh along or to actually send the link if you have it. Taking it seriously misses the point.
